why.support: Every text has a **purpose** (why), an **audience** (who) and a **context** (where and when). Spot them, and texts make sense. Use them, and your writing works.
why.core: Every text is shaped by three things: its **purpose** (why it was written), its **audience** (who it's for) and its **context** (where, when and what's going on). Spot those three, and you understand any text faster. Use them when you write, and your messages land the way you want, at work, at TAFE and in life.
why.extend: Purpose, audience and context determine a text's structure and language. Identifying them lets you interpret what a text is doing and why; applying them lets you make deliberate choices so your own texts are effective for the people and situations they're meant for.

articles.title: Read the room

body.support:
Ask three questions about any text.

**1. Purpose: why was it written?**

- to **inform**: give facts
- to **persuade**: make you do something
- to **instruct**: tell you how
- to **entertain**: make you feel something.

**2. Audience: who's it for?** A mate? A boss? Everyone? The words change. *running l8* to a mate. *Sorry, I'm running 10 minutes late* to a boss.

**3. Context: where and when?** On a phone? In a rush? In an emergency? Short, clear words help in a rush.

These three things shape how a text looks and sounds.

**Talk it through.** In a group, share what you notice. Build on what others say: *I agree, and…*
body.core:
Before you read or write anything, it helps to ask three questions.

**1. What's the purpose?** Why was it written? Most texts are trying to do one main job:

- **inform**: give facts (a timetable, a news report)
- **persuade**: make you think or do something (an ad, a petition)
- **instruct**: tell you how (a recipe, a safety procedure)
- **entertain**: make you feel something (a story, a funny video).

**2. Who's the audience?** Who is it for? A mate, a teacher, a boss, a customer, or the whole public? The audience changes the words. You'd write *running l8* to a mate, but *I'm running 10 minutes late, sorry* to your boss.

**3. What's the context?** Where, when and how will it be read? On a phone, in a hurry? Printed on a wall? During an emergency, when people are scared? Context changes the **length**, the **layout** and the **tone**. In a hurry, people need short, clear words. In an emergency, they need to know exactly what to do.

**Putting it together.** Purpose, audience and context work together to shape a text's **structure** (how it's organised) and its **language** (the words and tone). A formal email to a manager has a greeting, short paragraphs and a sign-off. A text to a mate might be one line and an emoji. Both can be right. It depends on the room.

**Talk it through.** These questions are great to discuss in a group. Different people notice different things. Listen, add your idea, and build on what others say: *I agree, and I also noticed…*
body.extend:
Every text is written for a reason, for someone, in a situation. Looking at those three things explains why a text looks and sounds the way it does.

**Purpose** is the text's job: to **inform**, **persuade**, **instruct** or **entertain**. Many texts do more than one, but one job usually comes first.

**Audience** is who the text is for. The writer's relationship with them (friend, boss, customer, the public) decides how **formal** or **informal** the language is, how much they explain, and what tone fits.

**Context** is the situation: the medium (phone, print, sign), the setting (work, home, an emergency), the time pressure, and how the reader might be feeling. A text read in a crisis must be clear and tell people what to do. A text read at leisure can include more detail.

Together, these shape a text's **structure** (how it's organised and laid out) and **language** (words, sentence length, tone). To judge whether a text is **effective**, ask whether those choices suit its purpose, audience and context.

Group discussion sharpens this. Different readers notice different things. Listening, and building on what others say (*I'd add that…*), gives a fuller reading than working alone.

caseStudies.title: One emergency, one set of words

body.support:
Emergency warnings used to be hard to follow. Each state used its own words and colours.

So Australia made the **Australian Warning System**. It started in **2021**.

It has **three levels**:

- **Advice** (yellow): *Stay informed.*
- **Watch and Act** (orange): *Get ready.*
- **Emergency Warning** (red): *Leave now.*

**Purpose**: keep people safe. **Audience**: everyone. **Context**: an emergency, read on a phone.

So the warnings are short. They use colour. They tell you what to do.
body.core:
For years, emergency warnings in Australia were confusing. Each state used its own words, colours and symbols for bushfires, floods and storms. If you moved interstate, or travelled, the warnings could look completely different.

So Australia created the **Australian Warning System**. It started rolling out in **2021**, and was adopted state by state over the next few years. It was developed with **community research**: emergency services asked people what they understood and what they needed.

The system has **three levels**, each with its own colour and a clear action:

- **Advice** (yellow): something has started. *Stay informed.*
- **Watch and Act** (orange): conditions are changing. *Prepare to leave.*
- **Emergency Warning** (red): you're in danger. *Leave now* or *Seek shelter now.*

Think about the **purpose**: to keep people safe. The **audience**: everyone, including people who are stressed, rushed or reading in a second language. The **context**: an emergency, often read on a phone.

That's why the warnings are short, use colour, and always tell you **what to do**. Every choice in the text comes from purpose, audience and context.
body.extend:
Before the **Australian Warning System**, emergency warnings were different in each state, and for each kind of hazard. Bushfires, floods and storms all used different words, colours and icons. That made warnings harder to follow for people who travel, move interstate or speak English as a second language.

The national system began rolling out in **2021**, and states and territories adopted it over the next few years. It was built on **community research** into how people understand warnings and act on them.

It has **three levels**. Each has a colour and an action:

- **Advice** (yellow): an incident has started. *Stay informed.*
- **Watch and Act** (orange): conditions are changing. For example, *prepare to leave*.
- **Emergency Warning** (red): danger is close. For example, *leave now* or *seek shelter now*.

The design comes straight from **purpose** (saving lives), **audience** (everyone, including people under stress or with limited English) and **context** (fast-moving emergencies, often read on phones). Short messages, colour codes and an action in every warning are choices made for that situation. There's one test of whether it works: do people know what to do?

model.text:
**The news:** I will be late to work tomorrow because of a dentist appointment.

**To my manager**

Hi Deb, I have a dentist appointment tomorrow at 8:30 am. I should be at work by 10. I am sorry for the short notice. I can stay until 5 to make up the time.

**To my workmate**

Hey Jai, I'm at the dentist tomorrow morning, in around 10. Can you grab the delivery if it comes early? I owe you one.

**What changed:** For my manager, I gave times and offered a fix. For Jai, I was casual and asked a favour. The purpose changed too. One informs, and one asks for help.

teacher.overview: Students learn to identify a text's purpose, audience and context, and to explain how these shape its structure and language. They annotate everyday and workplace texts, discuss them in small groups, and rewrite the same message for two audiences. The case study is the Australian Warning System, a national redesign of emergency warnings around purpose, audience and context. Extend students evaluate a text's effectiveness.
prep: Ask students to bring one real text each (flyers, signs, emails, ads, screenshots). Have spares.
Print the Australian Warning System icons, or show them on screen.
Plan groups of 3 or 4 for the Do it.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** inform, persuade, instruct, entertain. Audience changes formality, length and tone (e.g. *running l8* vs *I'm running 10 minutes late*). Context is where, when and how it's read (e.g. an emergency warning on a phone).

**Messages:** 1 informal (fine for a mate); 2 formal greeting with her name; 3 clear facts (why, how late, which shift); 4 a solution (reliable); 5 polite sign-off.

**Table (samples):** café job ad — inform/persuade; job seekers; a shop window, read in passing. Mate's text — entertain/inform; a friend; a phone, casual. Safety sign — instruct; workers and visitors; a building site, read quickly. Energy drink ad — persuade; young people; a phone feed. Council letter — inform; residents; at home.

**Case study:** each state used different words, colours and icons; e.g. colours are fast to read under stress (context), and simple words suit everyone (audience); because the purpose is to keep people safe, and people in danger need to know what to do.

realityCheck: **Emergencies can be personal.** Some students have lived through bushfires or floods. Check in before the case study.
**Real texts work best.** Students engage more with texts from their own lives, workplaces and towns.
**Formal isn't always better.** Make clear that informal is right for some audiences. The skill is choosing.
**Group work needs structure.** Give roles (reader, note-taker, reporter) so everyone contributes.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's a strong opener for the Text Toolkit, and links to Know Your Text Types.
